text: You've got a chart and environment-specific values. This last lesson of the chapter is about running that chart through a real lifecycle — upgrading it safely, rolling it back when something goes wrong, and keeping track of exactly what's deployed where.

In practice you almost never type helm install and helm upgrade as two separate commands. helm upgrade with the install flag creates the release if it doesn't exist and upgrades it if it does, so the same command works on day one and day one hundred. Wait makes Helm block until the Pods actually report ready. And atomic is the safety net — if the upgrade fails or that wait times out, Helm automatically rolls the release back to its previous working state instead of leaving the cluster half-upgraded.

Every install, upgrade, and rollback against a release creates a new numbered revision, and helm history lists every one of them — when it happened, which chart version, which app version, and its status. That's an ordered, queryable record a sed-and-kubectl-apply script never gave you.

When you need to go back to a known-good state, helm rollback re-applies an earlier revision's manifests and values — as a brand-new revision. History never gets erased, it just keeps growing, the same way it does on a normal upgrade. Leave off the revision number and it rolls back to whatever came immediately before.

Day to day, you'll lean on a small set of commands: helm list to see every release in a namespace, helm get values to see exactly what's actually in effect on a running release right now, and helm uninstall when a release needs to go away for good, history included.

That closes out Chapter 6. You went from copy-pasted YAML across environments, to a real templated chart, to per-environment values files, to a full upgrade-and-rollback workflow with a real audit trail behind it. Next chapter turns to securing the cluster itself — RBAC, pod security standards, and locking down the API server.
